goal.objective:
Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.

`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You implement one program task in the workspace you are given, against its own test suite, and you stop when the tests pass.

The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

5: /** Deterministic 32-bit PRNG so the generated paths replay identically. */
6: function mulberry32(seed) {
7:   let a = seed >>> 0;
8:   return function next() {
9:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
10:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
11:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
12:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
13:   };

{
  "id": "code:path-normalize",
  "tier": 2,
  "domain": "systems",
  "title": "POSIX path arithmetic without a filesystem",
  "prompt": "Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.\n\n`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.\n\n`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.\n\n`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`.",

Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.

`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.
